key_points.point: The document identifies that major AI organizations like OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic explicitly define their mission as the creation of AGI to benefit humanity. These organizations view AGI as a transformative force capable of solving existential problems and outperforming humans at economically valuable tasks. This goal serves as the primary driver for their research funding and strategic development. The document notes that these entities view AGI as a 'north-star' that justifies large-scale investment and development efforts.
key_points.verbatim: The mission statement of OpenAI is “. . . to ensure that [AGI] benefits all of humanity.” Its website (OpenAI, 2025a) states that “we are building safe and beneficial AGI, but will also consider our mission fulfilled if our work aids others to achieve this outcome.”
key_points.excerpt_context: Appendix A, Definitions of AGI and Related Concepts

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that AGI is widely conceptualized as a threshold where AI systems match or exceed human cognitive performance across broad domains. It catalogs various definitions, including those from OpenAI and Bostrom, which frame AGI as a transformative, high-capability state. This reflects the accelerationist belief in the imminence and significance of human-level AI.
key_points.verbatim: OpenAI’s mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence (AGI)—by which we mean highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work—benefits all of humanity.
key_points.excerpt_context: Table 1: Sample of proposed definitions of AGI and related concepts.

key_points.point: The authors argue that the AI research community has a unique responsibility to distinguish hype from reality, as AI outputs are deployed rapidly in ways that affect billions of people. This aligns with safetyist concerns regarding the societal impact of unconstrained AI deployment. The authors emphasize the need for evidence-based answers to questions about the merits of AI tools to prevent confusion and protect the public interest.
key_points.verbatim: The outputs of AI research are deployed as real-world products at a staggering pace, in proliferating contexts, affecting billions of people. This warrants urgent work on trusted, evidence-based answers to questions about the scientific, engineering, and societal merits of AI tools.

key_points.point: The document cites research that frames current and near-term AI systems as potential sources of existential risk. This perspective suggests that the trajectory of AI development, even in its current state, necessitates rigorous safety evaluation to prevent catastrophic outcomes. The inclusion of this literature indicates that the document acknowledges the safetyist concern that AI capabilities may outpace our ability to control them.
key_points.verbatim: Bucknall, B. S. and Dori-Hacohen, S. Current and NearTerm AI as a Potential Existential Risk Factor.

key_points.point: The document references research on the 'impossible safety' of large AI models, which posits that there are fundamental limits to ensuring the safety of these systems. This aligns with safetyist beliefs that current alignment techniques are insufficient to guarantee the behavior of increasingly complex models. It highlights a skepticism toward the idea that scaling alone will lead to safe, controllable systems.
key_points.verbatim: El-Mhamdi, E.-M., Farhadkhani, S., Guerraoui, R., Gupta, N., Hoang, L.-N., Pinot, R., Rouault, S., and Stephan, J. On the Impossible Safety of Large AI Models, May 2023.

key_points.point: The document highlights that influential AI leaders, such as Dario Amodei and Geoff Hinton, believe that AGI or 'powerful AI' systems with capabilities exceeding human experts will emerge in the near future. These leaders express concern regarding the societal implications of such systems, including the potential for biological humans to be relegated to a secondary status. The document acknowledges that these beliefs are central to the safety-oriented discourse within major AI labs.
key_points.verbatim: Geoff Hinton stated to Forbes (Maymin, 2023) that he “is certain we will have AGI soon, and biological humans will be relegated to be the second-smartest species on the planet.”
key_points.excerpt_context: Appendix A, Other Influential Executives & Researchers

key_points.point: The document cites Summerfield (2023) to argue that AI systems lacking a shared 'umwelt' (worldview) with humans will be unintelligible, leading to unreliability and safety risks. This aligns with safetyist concerns regarding the opacity and potential misalignment of advanced AI systems.
key_points.verbatim: If we build an AI that sees the world in a radically different way to us, its behaviour and mental states will be unintelligible. Such an agent will be at best unreliable and at worst unsafe.
key_points.excerpt_context: Table 1: Sample of proposed definitions of AGI and related concepts.

key_points.point: The authors argue that the AI research community should stop treating 'AGI' as a north-star goal because the term is ill-defined, contested, and serves as a source of hype rather than scientific progress. They propose that the community instead prioritize specific, measurable scientific and societal goals. This approach aims to strip away the quasi-religious or marketing-driven rhetoric surrounding AGI to ensure research is grounded in rigorous, verifiable science.
key_points.verbatim: Therefore, the AI research community needs to stop treating “AGI” as the north-star goal of AI research.

key_points.point: The authors identify 'Generality Debt' as a trap where the pursuit of vague, flexible AI tools postpones necessary engineering and scientific rigor. They argue that because 'generality' is poorly defined, it allows researchers to avoid specifying measurable properties, leading to flawed evaluation and a lack of external validity. This reflects the skeptic view that AI progress is often uneven and that claims of 'general' intelligence are frequently rhetorical rather than functional.
key_points.verbatim: We term this trap “Generality Debt” to parallel technical debt (Sculley et al., 2014): it delays the work that needs to be done as part of AI research which, if left undone, takes more work to address in the future.

key_points.point: The authors argue that current AI research often conflates engineering artifacts with scientific discovery, leading to 'bad science' where performance claims are presented without rigorous hypothesis testing. They suggest that the field should move away from SOTA-chasing and toward more deliberate, exploratory research. This supports the skeptic belief that AI development should be treated as an iterative, fallible process rather than a revolutionary march toward a singular AGI goal.
key_points.verbatim: As Hullman et al. (2022) point out, a “typical supervised ML paper” (e.g., one that reports accuracy metrics on a benchmark) is often just an “engineering artifact”, a tool attached to performance claims that cannot be refuted because of replication challenges.

key_points.point: The document argues that the AI community should prioritize the support and benefit of human beings as the primary goal of technology, rather than pursuing AGI as a north-star. It suggests that focusing on human needs allows for democratic deliberation and collective legitimacy, which are currently undermined by the industry's fixation on AGI. This approach shifts the focus from technological capability to social merit and human-centric outcomes.
key_points.verbatim: If the AI community nevertheless wants an overarching goal to strive towards, the goal should be the support and benefit of human beings. The goals of technology are shaped by people. Evidence-based approaches to examining whether technology effectively meets the needs of people—be they “users”, “consumers”, “patients”, “scholars”, or a myriad of business and social monikers—are well-established.

key_points.point: The document advocates for a pluralistic approach to AI research, recommending that the community articulate many worthwhile scientific, engineering, and societal goals rather than a single north-star. This pluralism is presented as a necessary response to the lack of consensus and the diverse values present in society. By embracing heterogeneity, the community can avoid the traps of arbitrary goal selection and exclusion.
key_points.verbatim: Rather than a single general north-star goal (or small set of goals), the AI community should articulate many worthwhile scientific, engineering, and societal goals—and many possible paths to fulfilling them. Reaching meaningful scientific and societal consensus on the goals of a field as broad-ranging as AI is challenging. When consensus may not be viable or desirable, we recommend pluralism: allowing multiple viable conceptions of the goals of AI research.

key_points.point: The document calls for greater inclusion of diverse communities and disciplines in the goal-setting process for AI research. It argues that excluding end users, domain experts, and those affected by research outcomes impoverishes the potential of AI to achieve worthwhile goals. Inclusion is framed as a mechanism to identify unintended consequences and ensure that technology decisions are justified to the public.
key_points.verbatim: Greater inclusion of communities and disciplines in shaping the goals of AI research is beneficial to innovation. Identifying worthwhile goals, related use cases, and potential unintended consequences depends on engaging diverse viewpoints. Within AI research, these viewpoints must include those of end users, experts from other fields, those affected by research outcomes, and data annotators.

key_points.point: The document highlights the environmental and resource-related costs of large-scale AI efforts, noting that these projects have detrimental impacts on the climate and reinforce existing resource disparities. It argues that the current focus on computational scale in AGI research exacerbates these issues, making it harder for smaller actors to participate in the field.
key_points.verbatim: Large-scale efforts also have detrimental impacts on climate, reinforcing resource disparities (Bucknall & Dori-Hacohen, 2022; Kaack et al., 2022; Luccioni et al., 2024).

key_points.point: The document includes references to research that critiques the 'bullshit' nature of LLMs, arguing that they lack genuine understanding. This supports the skeptic intention of framing AI as mere pattern matching rather than intelligent agents. By highlighting this work, the document reinforces the view that current AI hype is disconnected from the reality of the technology's capabilities.
key_points.verbatim: Hicks, M. T., Humphries, J., and Slater, J. ChatGPT is bullshit. Ethics and Information Technology, 26(2):38, June 2024.

key_points.point: The document cites foundational research on intersectional accuracy disparities in commercial AI, which serves as empirical evidence of systemic bias. This aligns with the skeptic belief that AI systems internalize and reproduce historical discriminatory patterns. The inclusion of this work emphasizes the need to focus on immediate, measurable harms rather than speculative AGI goals.
key_points.verbatim: Buolamwini, J. and Gebru, T. Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification.

key_points.point: The document references the 'TESCREAL' bundle, which critiques the ideological underpinnings of AGI research, specifically linking it to eugenics and utopianism. This supports the skeptic view that the pursuit of AGI is driven by problematic, historically-rooted ideologies rather than objective scientific progress. It frames the AGI 'north-star' as a social construct with potentially harmful consequences.
key_points.verbatim: Gebru, T. and Torres, E. P. The TESCREAL bundle: Eugenics and the promise of utopia through artificial general intelligence.

key_points.point: The document asserts that the definition of AGI is often used as a financial or strategic tool by corporations rather than a scientific one. It highlights that different organizations use varying, often vague, definitions of AGI to suit their specific mission statements or competitive goals. The authors advocate for a more pluralistic approach to intelligence that favors contextualism over the singular, ill-defined goal of AGI.
key_points.verbatim: We agree with Morris et al. (2024)’s proposal to broaden discussions of AGI definitions to include accounts that avoid the term “AGI” yet address similar goals of achieving human-level intelligence.
key_points.excerpt_context: Appendix A, Definitions of AGI and Related Concepts

key_points.point: The document argues that 'AGI' is a poorly defined, potentially sterile concept that functions more as a hype-driven 'North-star' than a scientifically rigorous goal. It advocates for moving away from monolithic AGI definitions toward context-specific, value-dependent, and pluralistic frameworks for measuring AI performance.
key_points.verbatim: Intelligence is a meaningless concept in and of itself. It requires a frame of reference, a specification of a domain of thought and action, in order to make it meaningful.
key_points.excerpt_context: Table 1: Sample of proposed definitions of AGI and related concepts.

key_points.point: The document supports defining intelligence through human-centric, value-dependent lenses rather than abstract, business-driven metrics. It highlights accounts that emphasize the interdependencies between agents, environments, and human measurers.
key_points.verbatim: Defines human and artificial intelligence as “value-dependent cognitive performance”, and “centres interdependencies between agents, their environments, and their measurers in collectively constructing and measuring context-specific performances of intelligent action.”
key_points.excerpt_context: Table 1: Sample of proposed definitions of AGI and related concepts.

factual_claims.claim: The term 'AGI' is used by researchers and corporations without a shared, scientifically grounded definition, creating an illusion of consensus that hinders productive goal setting.
OpenAI and Microsoft signed an agreement stating that OpenAI has only achieved AGI when it develops systems that can generate at least $100 billion in profits.
Computational resource requirements for training state-of-the-art AI models are doubling approximately every few months.

The pursuit of AGI as a primary research goal is increasingly criticized for its lack of scientific validity and its reliance on hype. Researchers argue that the term 'AGI' is ill-defined and that the focus on it distracts from addressing real-world harms and technical limitations in current machine learning.
OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic have explicitly stated missions centered on the development of AGI to benefit humanity.
Many AI researchers doubt or reject the goal of AGI, despite its prominence in corporate and policy discourse.
OpenAI and Microsoft reportedly signed an agreement in 2024 defining AGI as the development of AI systems capable of generating at least $100 billion in profits.
